vignette: Akua had always been drawn to working with children. As a tutor, she found joy in helping them grasp new concepts and watching their confidence grow. But it was precisely this setting that now filled her with dread. The sound of kids crying, which once would have prompted her to comfort and reassure, now sent her reeling. It started on days when the children were particularly restless or upset; Akua's stomach would churn with nausea as she struggled to focus on the lesson at hand. The incident that changed everything had occurred six months prior, during a tutoring session at a student's home. Her client's older brother, who was supposed to be studying in another room, had snuck up behind her and attacked her. The event still felt like it belonged to someone else - a hazy, disjointed sequence of moments that Akua couldn't quite piece together into a coherent narrative. When memories did surface, they brought back the same terror she'd experienced during the assault. In the aftermath, Akua found herself withdrawing from situations that might bring her happiness or hope. She stopped attending social gatherings with friends and family, fearing that someone would inadvertently ask about the incident or, worse still, try to offer comforting words that would only make her feel more vulnerable. Even her relationship with her partner began to fray as she pulled away from intimate conversations, terrified of being reminded of what had happened. Akua's mind was a maze of self-blame and recrimination. She couldn't shake the feeling that she was somehow responsible for the attack - that if only she'd been more vigilant or assertive, it wouldn't have occurred. This rumination consumed her every waking moment, making it impossible to concentrate on even the simplest tasks. Her partner, sensing Akua's growing despondency, tried to encourage her to seek help. But Akua was certain that if she delved into the traumatic event itself, she would be overwhelmed by emotions she couldn't handle. She felt like she was barely holding on as it was - any slight upset might send her tumbling over the edge. As the weeks turned into months, Akua's relationships began to suffer. Her partner grew frustrated with her increasing withdrawal; friends and family expressed concern about her growing isolation. Even her work as a tutor became strained, as she found herself less patient and more irritable around the very children she had once loved working with. It was only when Akua realized that she might lose everything - her relationship, her job, even her sense of self - that she finally sought help. She was desperate to break free from this prison of fear and recrimination, but a part of her remained terrified that confronting the trauma head-on would be too much to bear. As she sat in the therapist's office, Akua couldn't help but wonder if it was already too late - or if there was still a way back to the person she once was.
